title: Ψύλλα καὶ ἀθλητής
part: The Flea and the Athlete (Chambry 356 · Perry 231)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 356 (= Perry 231). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ψύλλα ποτὲ πηδήσασα ἐκάθισεν ἐπὶ ταρσοῦ ποδὸς ἀνδρὸς ἀθλητοῦ νοσοῦντος καὶ ἀλλομένη ἐνῆκε δῆγμα.
sentences.tr: Psylla pote pēdēsasa ekathisen epi tarsou podos andros athlētou nosountos kai allomenē enēke dēgma.
sentences.l: A flea once, having leapt, settled on the flat of the foot of a man, an athlete who was ailing, and, springing about, drove in a bite.
sentences.i: A flea once leapt and settled on the flat of an ailing athlete's foot, and as it sprang about it drove in its bite.
sentences.n: ὁ ταρσὸς τοῦ ποδός is the flat of the foot. ἐνίημι, 'send in', takes δῆγμα, 'a bite', as its object: Greek puts the bite in where English simply bites. νοσοῦντος is not idle — the athlete is already unwell.

sentences.t: Ὁ δ’ ἀκροχολήσας εὐτρεπίσας τοὺς ὄνυχας οἷός τε ἦν συνθλάσαι τὴν ψύλλαν.
sentences.tr: Ho d’ akrocholēsas eutrepisas tous onychas hoios te ēn synthlasai tēn psyllan.
sentences.l: And he, having flown into a rage, having made his nails ready, was in a position to crush the flea.
sentences.i: The man flew into a temper, got his nails ready, and was all set to crush the flea.
sentences.n: οἷός τε εἶναι with the infinitive is the standing idiom for 'to be able, be in a position to'. ἀκροχολέω is to be quick to anger — the bile rising at the very tip. Two aorist participles run one after the other before the main verb, the ordinary engine of these stories.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ ὑφ’ ὁρμῆς φυσικὸν πήδημα λαβοῦσα ἀπέδρα τοῦ θανεῖν ἀπαλλαγεῖσα.
sentences.tr: Hē de hyph’ hormēs physikon pēdēma labousa apedra tou thanein apallageisa.
sentences.l: But she, by an impulse taking her natural leap, ran off, released from dying.
sentences.i: But the flea, under an impulse, took her natural leap and got clean away, and so escaped death.
sentences.n: τοῦ θανεῖν is an articular infinitive in the genitive after ἀπαλλαγεῖσα, 'set free from' — Greek turns a whole verb into a noun with nothing but the article. ὑπό with the genitive gives the moving cause, 'under an impulse'. ἀποδιδράσκω is the verb regularly used of a slave running away.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὃς στενάξας εἶπεν· « Ὦ Ἡράκλεις, ὅταν πρὸς ψύλλαν οὕτω ⟨συμμαχῇς⟩, πῶς ἐπὶ τοὺς ἀνταγωνιστὰς συνεργὸς ἔσῃ ; »
sentences.tr: Kai hos stenaxas eipen· « Ō Hērakleis, hotan pros psyllan houtō ⟨symmachēis⟩, pōs epi tous antagōnistas synergos esēi ; »
sentences.l: And he, having groaned, said: « O Heracles, when against a flea you ⟨fight at my side⟩ like this, how will you be a helper against my adversaries? »
sentences.i: And the man groaned and said: « O Heracles, if this is your alliance against a flea, what help will you be against my opponents? »
sentences.n: Heracles is the patron of athletes, the god a wrestler counts on; but ὦ Ἡράκλεις is also the ordinary Greek cry of exasperation, and the joke lives in both senses at once. ⟨συμμαχῇς⟩ stands in Chambry's angle brackets: the verb is his supplement, not what the manuscripts give, so the shape of the complaint is reconstructed. ὅταν with the subjunctive is the indefinite 'whenever'. Καὶ ὅς is the old use of the relative as a demonstrative, 'and he'.

sentences.t: Ἀτὰρ οὖν καὶ ἡμᾶς ὁ λόγος διδάσκει μὴ δεῖν ἐπὶ τὰ ἐλάχιστα καὶ ἀκίνδυνα πράγματα ἐπευθὺς τοὺς θεοὺς ἀνακαλεῖν, ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ τὰς μείζους ἀνάγκας.
sentences.tr: Atar oun kai hēmas ho logos didaskei mē dein epi ta elachista kai akindyna pragmata epeuthys tous theous anakalein, all’ epi tas meizous anankas.
sentences.l: So then the story teaches us too that we must not, over the smallest and harmless matters, call at once upon the gods, but over the greater straits.
sentences.i: So then the story teaches us too not to call the gods in at once over the smallest matters, where nothing is at risk, but only in graver need.
sentences.n: Two closing formulas folded into one: Ἀτὰρ οὖν καὶ ἡμᾶς, 'so then we too', which turns the fable round on the reader (fables 23, 60, 163, 245, 272, 284), and ὁ λόγος διδάσκει, 'the story teaches'. μὴ δεῖν is δεῖ in the infinitive after διδάσκει, negated by μή as infinitives are. ἐπευθύς is a rare strengthened form of εὐθύς, 'straight away'.
